facts.text: Amankora arrived in 2004 as the first international hospitality brand permitted to operate in Bhutan.
facts.excerpt: Amankora, as it became known, arrived in 2004 as the first international hospitality brand ever permitted to operate in the country.

facts.text: The late Kerry Hill designed the lodges in the government-mandated style of whitewashed rammed-earth walls and wooden-framed windows.
facts.excerpt: The late Kerry Hill was brought in to design the lodges in the government-mandated style of whitewashed rammed-earth walls and wooden-framed windows.

facts.text: Amankora is a circuit through Bhutan broken across five lodges among the Himalayas.
facts.excerpt: A stay at Amankora is a slow pilgrimage circuit through Bhutan, broken across five lodges among the Himalayas.

facts.text: The Paro lodge opened first, with the full five-lodge circuit completed three years later.
facts.excerpt: The Paro lodge opened first, with the full five-property circuit completed three years later.

facts.text: The open-plan bedrooms at Amankora Paro have a king-size bed, a wood-burning stove and banquette window seating.
facts.excerpt: Open-plan bedrooms feature a king-size bed, wood-burning stove and banquette window seating

facts.text: Amankora Paro has views of the snow-covered Jhomolhari mountain.
facts.excerpt: Views of the snow-covered Jhomolhari mountain

facts.text: The Amankora Paro dining room has a terrace overlooking the 17th-century Drukgyel Dzong.
facts.excerpt: Dining room with terrace overlooking the 17th-century Drukgyel Dzong

facts.text: The Paro spa has two storeys, five treatment rooms, a hot stone bath, sauna, steam room and yoga studio.
facts.excerpt: Two-storey spa with five treatment rooms, hot stone bath, sauna, steam room and yoga studio

facts.text: The Himalayan Hot Stone Bath uses heated river stones lowered into the bath, and local Khempa herbs infuse the water.
facts.excerpt: Inspired by a tradition, where river stones are heated and lowered into the bath to release beneficial minerals, while local Khempa herbs infuse the water with their healing properties.

facts.text: After the hike to Tiger's Nest, guests can have a recovery lunch at Amankora's Log Cabin in the shadow of the monastery.
facts.excerpt: Conclude the hike to Bhutan’s holiest pilgrimage site with a rejuvenating lunch in the shadows of the Tiger’s Nest at Amankora’s atmospheric Log Cabin

facts.text: The hike to Taktsang (Tiger's Nest) takes four hours and reaches a 7th-century monastery on the mountainside.
facts.excerpt: Embark on the exhilarating four-hour hike to the Tiger’s Nest, the iconic 7th-century monastery that clings to the mountainside, 900 metres above the valley floor.

facts.text: Guests can light 108 butter lamps at Kyichu Lhakhang, a temple that dates to the 7th century.
facts.excerpt: Take part in the symbolic lighting of 108 butter lamps at one of Bhutan's oldest temples, Kyichu Lhakhang, which dates to the 7th century.

facts.text: A complimentary morning breathwork and asana session is held in the lodge's yoga studio, suitable for all abilities.
facts.excerpt: Enjoy a complimentary morning breathwork and _asana_ (yoga poses) session in the lodge’s studio, hosted by an experienced teacher and suitable for all abilities.

facts.text: At each lodge restaurant there is an a la carte of Western and fusion dishes plus a rotating set menu that alternates between Bhutanese and another Asian cuisine, Indian at Paro.
facts.excerpt: a rotating set menu that alternates between Bhutanese and another Asian cuisine (Indian at Paro, Thai at Thimphu)

facts.text: Most ingredients come from local farmers and the lodges' own kitchen gardens.
facts.excerpt: Most ingredients come from local farmers and the lodges' own kitchen gardens

facts.text: Food and beverages are all-inclusive, covering local Bhutanese beers and whisky; only top-shelf spirits cost extra.
facts.excerpt: Food and beverages are all-inclusive, with an extensive drink list that covers local Bhutanese beers and whisky (only top-shelf spirits cost extra).

facts.text: There are no televisions in any room, nor a mini-bar.
facts.excerpt: There are no televisions in any room, nor a mini-bar.

facts.text: The lodges have no conventional lobby or check-in desk, and no signage.
facts.excerpt: None of the lodges have a conventional lobby or check-in desk, nor any signage.

facts.text: Any trip to Bhutan requires a licensed guide and driver, which Amankora can arrange but guests are not required to book through it.
facts.excerpt: Any trip to the kingdom requires a licensed guide and driver, which Amankora can arrange, but isn't required to book through.

facts.text: Tiger's Nest is a quick drive from the Paro lodge, as is the National Museum of Bhutan, housed inside a 17th-century watchtower.
facts.excerpt: In Paro, Tiger's Nest (the country's signature hike) is a quick drive away, as is the National Museum of Bhutan, housed inside a 17th-century watchtower.

facts.text: Condé Nast Traveler says spring and autumn are the best times to visit, as summer monsoons can wash out hikes and winter is too cold for the trails.
facts.excerpt: Springtime and autumn months are the best windows to visit. Summer monsoons can wash out hikes, while winter brings too much cold for the trails.

facts.text: Travelers should expect long transfers to reach the lodges.
facts.excerpt: The common thread: a tolerance for long transfers to get here.

facts.text: The Banya Spa House sits in Paro's pine forest, uses oak- or birch-leaf bundles, and has an outdoor terrace with a cold plunge.
facts.excerpt: Set amid Paro’s pine forest, the Banya Spa House draws on Eastern European and Scandinavian traditions with oak- or birch-leaf bundles used to massage, stimulate and exfoliate

facts.text: Paro and Punakha lodges were to be closed through September 2026 for renovations; reopening not confirmed.
facts.excerpt: the Paro and Punakha locations will both be closed through September 2026 for extensive renovations.
